transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-05-06 16:00 PDT; duration 46m; attendees: James Kim, Priya Nair (Redwood), Liam O'Connor, Ava Rodriguez, Diego Santos (Aurora)

Summary: quick Optimize walkthrough — focus on batching, KV cache, and cost model for Aurora's payments use cases.

[00:00] James Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm James from Redwood, this is Priya our solutions engineer. We sent the deck, but we'll jump right into the Optimize walkthrough. Can you hear us ok?

[00:12] Liam O'Connor: Yeah, loud and clear. thanks James. quick context — we're trying to instrument NLU and chat responses in our payments UI; typical conversation length is short, like 40 to 120 tokens, but we have lots of concurrent small requests. Our primary concern is tail latency and cost.

[00:30] Priya Nair: Great, that's exactly what Optimize helps with. we'll cover batching, prefix caching (kv cache), and a cost model that shows token-level economics. One note — some transcriber words may be off, so forgive any typos.

[00:45] Priya Nair: starting with batching: there are two knobs — batch size ceiling and latency bucket. For low-latency apps we use small micro-batches plus continuous batching to fill under a 50-150ms window; for high throughput you can increase the window and reduce cost per token.

[01:15] Diego Santos: what's the typical latency trade on gpus? we run T4s in house but are open to dedicated from Redwood.

[01:25] Priya Nair: on modern A100-like nodes we see amortized per-token cost a lot lower, but tail latency can increase if you wait too long for batches. With continuous batching in our runtime we keep 95th percentile pretty stable — you can set a max wait of, say, 40ms and a min batch threshold to avoid single-request execution. For T4-like hardware the sweet spot is smaller windows.

[01:55] Liam O'Connor: ok, and KV cache — can you explain prefix vs KV cache? our prompts are short but often reuse conversation system messages.

[02:05] Priya Nair: sure — prefix cache is simple: cache the left-most tokens (system + static instructions) and reuse their activations; KV cache stores past key/value tensors for the decoder so subsequent tokens don't recompute previous context. For Aurora's case where you have lots of identical system prompts and short completions, prefix caching will give big wins — high hit rate on the static portions. KV cache helps more for long chats where you paginate or stream many tokens.

[02:45] Ava Rodriguez: how do we estimate hit rate? we have templated prompts with a per-customer variation like account id and small dynamic fields.

[02:55] Priya Nair: good question — Optimize's profiler can sample your live request set and estimate prefix similarity. if your only varying fields are short IDs in predictable spots, the prefix hit rate is often 60-85%. If the variable is mid-prompt free text, the hit rate drops. the cost model spreadsheet we'll send shows baseline, conservative, and optimistic hit-rate scenarios.

[03:25] James Kim: i'll show a quick slide with the cost math. The model inputs are: avg tokens/request, model throughput (tokens/sec), batch fill efficiency, cache hit rate, and infra hourly rates. we convert to $/k tokens and show delta vs baseline.

[03:50] Priya Nair: Example: with 70% prefix hit and 4x batching efficiency you can see up to 40-55% reduction in per-token cost on hosted runtime, with negligible impact to median latency. But important caveat — if you over-batch and set a long max-wait, tail latency can spike and user experience suffers.

[04:15] Diego Santos: what's the operational burden? how do we manage cache invalidation for per-customer system messages?

[04:25] Priya Nair: We support cache scoping by tenant. prefix cache keys include prompt hash and tenant id so when you rotate system content you can flush by key prefix or by TTL. TTLs are configurable; for security-sensitive changes you can trigger an explicit eviction through the API or via the Console.

[04:50] Liam O'Connor: we have strict PII rules — everything has to go through our KMS and logs must be redacted. how does Redwood handle encryption and audit logs?

[05:00] James Kim: short answer: SOC2 and enterprise customers can use Private deployment or Dedicated with VPC peering; we have KMS integrations for model payload encryption at rest and audit logs exported to your SIEM. We'll send the SOC2 report and our network architecture doc after the call.

[05:20] Ava Rodriguez: When you say dedicated, are we looking at guaranteed capacity or burstable? we want a baseline for daytime and spikes at month-end.

[05:30] Priya Nair: you can do reserved capacity for baseline throughput and enable burst capacity for spikes. the pricing model differs — reserved commit gives much lower unit costs. For the pilot we usually provision a small dedicated pool to reproduce latency and cost figures and then scale.

[05:50] James Kim: back to the cost model: here's an illustrative calc — assumptions: avg prompt 80 tokens, completion 60 tokens, batching gives 3x token amortization, prefix hit 65%. with Redwood hosted rates this maps to about $8/1M tokens vs $17/1M tokens without caching/batching — so roughly 52% savings in that scenario. again, we'll send CSVs with detailed numbers.

[06:25] Diego Santos: are these numbers including KV cache memory overhead? for long-lived KV entries we'll need more RAM.

[06:35] Priya Nair: yes the finer model includes memory and GPU utilization; KV cache will increase memory pressure which can reduce batch sizes if you're not on large GPUs. the spreadsheet has a column for extra GPU memory needed and estimated instance SKU changes. For prefix caching overhead is minimal since it's about reusing activations not holding full KV for many sessions.

[07:05] Liam O'Connor: what about correctness/regression risk? if we cache prefixes are we potentially masking model updates or rollout issues?

[07:15] Priya Nair: good point — Optimize ties cache retention to model versioning and rollout policies. when you roll a model we invalidate caches scoped to the old variant automatically or run parallel rollouts and shadow traffic to verify quality. we also have eval hooks to run your prompt set against new models before full cutover.

[07:45] Ava Rodriguez: ok sounds promising. what's a realistic pilot timeline?

[07:50] James Kim: typical pilot is 2-4 weeks: week 1 gather sample prompts and run profiler, week 2 run benchmarks + tune batching/cache params, week 3 run production-like pilot in a sandbox with dedicated capacity, week 4 evaluate results and finalize pricing.

[08:10] Diego Santos: any blockers on our side? we use on-prem GPU pool behind a firewall; we'd prefer Redwood Private but could also connect via VPC peering to Dedicated.

[08:22] Priya Nair: Private is an option; that takes longer to stand up (~4-6 weeks) for on-prem integration. VPC peering to Dedicated is faster and still meets most compliance needs. We'll note that in next steps.

[08:40] Liam O'Connor: can you run a quick demo of the Console profiler?

[08:45] Priya Nair: sure, sharing screen now — apologies if the transcriber mislabels some UI bits. here we see request distributions, token histograms, and a suggested batch/window setting. the profiler highlights top prompt templates and gives an estimated prefix hit. you can tweak the cache scope and simulate cost impact.

[10:15] Priya Nair: (demo audio) so clicking "Simulate" we can pick hit rates 40/60/80% and see cost delta. also toggling batch max-wait from 20ms to 80ms shows latency percentile changes.

[12:05] James Kim: quick Q from our side — what's the number one metric Aurora wants to optimize? is it cost, p95 latency, or error rate?

[12:15] Ava Rodriguez: p95 latency under 250ms is mandatory, cost is secondary but we need to reduce runway burn.

[12:25] James Kim: got it. we'll tune pilot to prioritize p95 under 200-250ms and show cost delta.

[12:35] Priya Nair: last section — ops runbook: we'll provide CLI commands to enable prefix caching, sample configs for batch windows, and eviction commands. also will include recommended TTLs per tenant.

[13:00] Diego Santos: would love the CLI snippets.

[13:05] Priya Nair: noted — action item.

[13:12] James Kim: final recap — we'll send the cost model, SOC2/network/KMS docs, pilot proposal and schedule. next meeting to lock pilot scope tentatively 2027-05-17. any final questions?

[13:28] Ava Rodriguez: none from me, thanks.

[13:32] Liam O'Connor: thank you, appreciate the walkthrough.

[13:35] James Kim: thanks everyone, we'll follow up by end of day tomorrow with materials.

[13:40] (call ends)

Note: transcript contains occasional misattributions and small transcription errors typical of automated meeting exports.
